[46] Tank, Exp: lab tests PCM RT 44HC 14% N/A active 𝑄𝑄𝑐𝑐𝑎𝑎𝑝𝑝 HP-TES Controls Strategies HP-TES system architecture is not the only contributing factor to peak load reduction and annual energy consumption; system controls play a significant role in determining the peak load reduction and shifting capabilities. While most control strategies come from chiller-ice systems, it is important to understand: (1) the control hierarchy, (2) control algorithms and approaches, and (3) their impact on demand reduction and energy consumption. Thus, in HP-TES system controls, three categories need to be considered: (1) discharge control, (2) recharge control, and (3) building loads. Controls can be classified into two levels: (1) traditional component-level controls, and (2) advanced system-level controls [15]. Traditional controls are the most straightforward, including on/off and PID controls. “On/Off controls”, also known as “bang-bang controls” [1], are used when a setpoint temperature is specified. For example, Lin et al. [47], [48] modeled and experimentally tested an underfloor PCM integrated with an electric heater. The electric heater was turned on when indoor conditions were below 18°C, and off when above 20°C. However, PID and on/off-based controls are simplistic and cannot control complex HP- TES architectures with several operating modes, especially during daily or hourly operations. Thus, a higher level of controls is required to operate the appropriate mode at the necessary period (i.e., peak hours for TES discharge, off-peak hours for recharging, etc.), while maintaining indoor setpoint conditions for thermal comfort. This level of control, supervisory control, can be categorized into several classes: simplified static control strategies and advanced dynamic controls [15], [34], [49]. In simplified static control strategies, the main control strategies were identified from the literature: (i) TES priori, (ii) chiller priori, (iii) constant proportion (partial chiller & TES), and (iv) rule-based controls. In TES priori systems, the ice/PCM tank is fully utilized during peak hours for space cooling when the chiller is off, or it can be activated to meet any additional building loads that the TES cannot cover. On the other hand, chiller priori controls correspond to the chiller running at its nominal capacity, and the TES is used to cover any excess building loads. In constant proportion (partial chiller/partial TES), the chiller and TES are set to operate with a fraction of their capacities to meet the required building load (e.g., 40% chiller capacity, 60% TES capacity). For each of these control techniques, the sizing of the TES and chiller may differ based on the required building loads, recharge loads, and the peak load ratios that both the TES and chiller must cover [34], [50], [51], [52].
